issues.issue: The effective date is left as a blank line, so the instrument does not state when it takes effect.

Section 2.15 defines 'Effective Date' as 'the date first stated above', but the preamble states no date, leaving every deadline keyed to the Effective Date (4.1.10, 4.9.4, 10.3.3) without a starting point.

This recital describes the MTC Network as 'currently planned' with approximate figures, which could be set against the operative definition in Section 2.38 and the Commencement Date test in Section 2.8.
This recital of the Operator's skill could be set against the operative warranties in Section 5.1.6 and 5.1.7, but they point the same way.
The recital lists services 'among other things', a general catch-all against enumerated specifics whose reach is not fixed.
This recital's description of services could be argued against the operative scope of 'Services' in Section 2.60 and Article 4.
'functions, responsibilities and tasks ... otherwise commonly performed by a dark fiber and lit network provider' is an open-ended standard with no fixed boundary.
This recital's open-ended scope sits against Section 4.7.1, which sweeps unlisted tasks into the Services, and could be used to expand or limit Article 4 obligations.

The rule that all capitalized terms are defined in Article 2 is contradicted by capitalized terms used but never defined there, such as 'Applicable Third Party' (7.3.2, 7.5), 'Governmental Authority' (7.3, 7.5), 'Attachment Database' (4.3.4) and 'CAPEX Upgrade and Update Fund' (4.6.1).
Section 11.1.3 refers repeatedly to 'the Rules' rather than the defined 'AAA Rules', but the reference is readily harmonised.
'Control' is used to define 'Affiliate' without any ownership or voting threshold, leaving the boundary of the term uncertain.
Section 8.1.4 supplies a 50% voting-securities test for 'change of control' while this definition supplies none, so 'control' bears two possible measures in one instrument.
'the initial four empty conduit' and 'for any purpose consistent with the uses granted' leave the scope of qualifying alterations imprecise.
The definition cross-refers to Section 4.9.2, which governs agreements between MTC and third parties; the Annual Plan is actually required by Section 4.9.3.2.
The cross-reference cannot be reconciled with Section 4.9.3.2, which is the provision that actually requires the Annual Plan.
The list of CAIs may be revised 'in MTC's sole discretion up until the Commencement Date', but the term's content after that date is not addressed.
The CAI count drives the Commencement Date test in Section 2.8 and the payment reduction in Section 4.9.2.8, so unilateral revision of Exhibit A moves those triggers.
Limb (a) requires both 90% of mileage 'the Design-Build Contractor is engaged to construct' and 90% of CAIs connected, and the denominator for each is not fixed.
Section 4.9.2.8 assumes clause (a) may not occur until after thirty months even though clause (b) makes thirty months itself a Commencement Date, so the two provisions pull against each other.

'would reasonably be understood by the Parties, to be proprietary or confidential' plus a non-exhaustive list ('may include, but is not necessarily limited to') leaves the boundary of protected information uncertain.
The definition makes information of either Party confidential, while Section 7.3.4 declares all written materials containing Confidential Information the sole property of MTC.

A Dark Fiber Customer is defined as leasing 'from MTC', but Section 4.7.4.4 has the Network Operator execute extension leases in its own name and Section 4.7.4.5 splits payments received by the Operator.

The definition points to 'the date first stated above', but the preamble leaves the date blank, so the Effective Date on which Sections 4.1.10, 4.9.4 and 10.3.3 all depend is not ascertainable from the instrument.
'any financial statements of Network Operator delivered to MTC' is circular, defining the term by the act of delivery rather than by content.
'or other similar casualty, or other substantial and extraordinary accidents' is a general catch-all following a long enumerated list, raising an ejusdem generis question about its reach.
The definition contemplates 'mediation, arbitration, legal and/or administrative action', which sits against Article 11's requirement that all disputes go to arbitration.
Indemnified Parties include non-signatories such as Affiliates and successors, which sits against Section 12.11's statement that no rights are conferred on non-parties.
'the Party from which another person seeks or is entitled to indemnification' is drafted so that a mere unfounded demand makes a Party an Indemnifying Party.
'any of the rating factors used to measure performance ... in critical areas' is entirely circular and identifies no fixed set of indicators.
KPIs are to be in Exhibit E per the exhibit list and Section 4.13.1, but that SLA was unfinished at signing, so the measures against which performance is judged were not fixed.
'funded in whole or in part by MTC' gives no minimum share, so an extension with token MTC funding qualifies.
Section 4.5.7 provides that MTC owns any MBI Network Extension 'regardless of the source of its funding', which cannot be squared with a definition that requires MTC funding.

The definition mixes an operative statement ('as built or acquired ... including any MBI Network Extensions and IRUs') with descriptive planning figures ('currently planned as a 1,338-mile'), leaving the actual boundary of the asset uncertain.

Section 2.39 says a fiber extension becomes part of the MTC Network unless it is a Network Extension and the Operator proves otherwise, which pulls against a definition fixed at what was 'built or acquired by the MassBroadband 123 Project'.

The second sentence is circular: an extension becomes part of the MTC Network unless it is a Network Extension and the Operator establishes 'that it is not or does not become part of the MTC Network', so the test defines itself.
This default cannot be squared with Section 4.5.5, which makes Network Operator Network Extensions 'the sole property of the Network Operator'.
The definition captures only Axia NGNetworks USA, Inc., while Section 9.1 extends 'Network Operator' to subcontractors and assignees for indemnity purposes.
The heading of Section 3.6 speaks of rights 'Upon Termination or Expiration', but Section 3.6.1 grants them only 'upon expiration of the Term'.
'funded and owned by the Network Operator but excludes any Network Extension funded by MTC' does not say what happens to an extension funded jointly.
Section 2.36 defines MBI Network Extensions as those funded 'in whole or in part' by MTC, so a partly-Operator-funded extension can answer both definitions.
'similar services on the MTC Network' fixes the deemed fee by reference to an undefined comparison, and the illustrative example does not resolve which services are similar.
Section 2.45 includes deemed Extension Fees in Network Revenue while excluding '(z) services on Network Operator Network Extensions', so the same activity is both counted and excluded.
'plus any additional policies reasonably required by MTC to meet legal requirements' allows MTC to expand the set of binding policies unilaterally, and 'At present this is includes' is ungrammatical.
Section 4.12 requires 'full compliance with all Network Policies' even though the set can grow by MTC's later action under this definition.

The sweeping catch-all — 'Any amounts earned ... from services related to the MTC Network, other than the categories expressly excluded ... shall be Network Revenue' — sits against a specific enumerated list of inclusions and exclusions, so the reach of the general words is contestable.

Limb (b) includes deemed Network Operator Network Extension Fees while exclusion (z) excludes 'services on Network Operator Network Extensions', an inconsistency that also drives the revenue-share calculation under Section 4.9.5.
After construction, a Network Segment exists only 'by mutual agreement', so no Segment can be defined if the Parties disagree.
Section 3.6.1.5(b) prices dark fiber by 'the highest number of strands leased in any Network Segment', a calculation that depends on agreement that may never be reached.
'the contents of which shall be binding upon the entity' is unusual and does not say what legal consequence follows from a certificate later shown to be inaccurate.
Because 'Party' is limited to MTC and the Network Operator, Article 11's arbitration of disputes 'between the Parties' does not obviously reach the parent guarantor required by Section 12.14.
The definition places the Price Caps in Exhibit F, but the Agreement's exhibit list assigns Price Caps to Exhibit D and Exhibit F to the Master Services Agreement with EOPSS and ITD.
'additional custom quotations for non-standard customer requests' and prices set 'in its sole discretion' for extension customers leave the boundary between regulated and unregulated pricing unclear.
The carve-out for extension customers conflicts with Section 4.7.2, which caps all Wholesale Service rates at the Price Caps regardless of where the customer connects.
'Renewal Decision' is defined by reference to requirements in Section 3.2, but Section 3.2 contains no decision requirements and the defined term is never used elsewhere in the Agreement.
Sections 3.6.1.2, 3.6.1.3 and 3.6.1.4 all speak of a 'Request for Renewal' rather than the defined 'Renewal Request', leaving it arguable whether the same instrument is meant.
Defining 'Retail Service' as 'services provided by a Third Party Service Provider' is circular and identifies the service by its provider rather than its character.

Because Section 2.64 defines a Third Party Service Provider as any organization 'other than Network Operator', Section 4.8's prohibition on the Operator providing Retail Services is definitionally impossible.
'routine scheduled maintenance ... as described herein' is defined by reference to itself and to an inclusive example.
'all performance obligations of the Network Operator hereunder' is a wholly general definition with no boundary of its own.
Section 4.7.1 further sweeps in tasks 'whether or not specifically described in this Agreement', so the scope of Services is set by an implication test rather than by this definition.
The SLA to be attached as Exhibit E was, per Section 4.13.1, still being negotiated at signing, so the standards this definition presupposes did not exist.

Section 8.4.1 says the Term shall not 'be deemed to have expired or terminated' until transfer assistance is complete, which cannot be squared with a Term that ends on expiration or termination under Section 3.1.

The list 'shall include, without limitation, ISPs, fiber companies, cable TV companies ...' is a general term followed by specifics, and the closing qualifier 'receiving Wholesale Service from the Network Operator' may or may not limit every listed category.
'lit transmission service of not less than 10 Gbps to an institutional customer without protocol' uses 'without protocol' and 'institutional customer', neither of which has any settled meaning here.

Limb (c) covers institutional customers who are not Third Party Service Providers, which sits awkwardly with Section 4.8's bar on the Operator providing retail service and with Section 2.66's list of Wholesale Customers.

The Term ends on the tenth anniversary of the Commencement Date, but Section 8.4.1 provides that the Term is not deemed to expire until services transfer assistance is complete, and Section 8.4.3 allows a further year's extension.
Section 2.54 defines a 'Renewal Decision' as a decision 'conforming to the requirements of Section 3.2', but this Section imposes no decision requirements at all.

The window 'from thirty (30) to thirty-two (32) months prior to expiration' is stated as a period running backwards, and combined with 'time being of the essence' the consequence of a late request is not stated.
Section 3.6.1.3(d) contemplates the consequences of neither Party issuing a Request for Renewal, so the failure to request has price consequences this Section does not mention.
Negotiations may be terminated 'at any time after the date that is twenty-eight (28) months prior to expiration', which leaves the earlier two-month period locked in without saying so expressly.
'five (5) anniversaries after the commencement of the last agreed Renewal Term' is an unusual formulation for a five-year period.
The rights arise 'upon expiration of the Term' subject to cure of 'any existing defaults', without saying who determines whether a default exists or how a disputed default affects the right.

The heading of Section 3.6 promises rights 'Upon Termination or Expiration' and Section 3.6.1.8 dates the lease from 'termination or expiration', yet this operative text confers rights only on expiration.
'between four (4) and eight (8) strands' with a maximum capped at ten percent of strands 'in any given portion' does not say who selects the number or how 'portion' is measured.
The exclusion is keyed to strand counts 'as of the Termination Date', a term used nowhere else and inconsistent with Section 3.6.1, which grants the right only on expiration of the Term.
The measurement period runs to 'the last calendar quarter before the date of the Request for Renewal', which is undefined and may never occur if no request is made.
Section 3.6.1.3(d) expressly contemplates that neither Party issues a Request for Renewal, in which case this Section's measurement date does not exist.
The table's discount is computed on 'invested' amounts that include an accumulated net operating loss under 3.6.1.2(b), so 'investment' is defined to include losses as well as expenditures.
Section 3.6.1.7 caps total discounts at $6,000,000 while this table can generate larger discounts on investments well above $10,000,000, so the two must be reconciled.
The table begins at 'At least $3,000,000' and supplies no price where the Operator has invested less than that amount.
Section 3.6.2 removes the rights entirely where the Operator declines renewal and has invested less than $3,000,000, so the gap in this table is filled only by reading the two together.
The provision cross-refers to 'Section 3.6.1.3 or 3.1.6.4', a transposed citation that does not exist, and to 'the same methodology as in Section 4.9.4' when the methodology is in Section 4.9.4.2.
Section 3.6.1.10 uses 'the CPI as in Section 4.9.4.2' for the same adjustment mechanism, showing the citation here is astray.
Pricing on 'the highest number of strands leased in any Network Segment' does not say whether that number is multiplied across the whole network or applied once.
Section 3.6.1.11 makes disclaimed strands void and excludes disclaimed mileage from cost shares, which pulls against pricing the exercise 'regardless of disclaimers of use'.

Payment is due 'on or before the end of the Term', yet Section 3.6.1 makes the right arise only upon expiration of the Term and Section 8.4.1 says the Term is not deemed to end until transfer assistance is complete.
The $6,000,000 cap cannot be squared with the tables in Sections 3.6.1.3 and 3.6.1.4, which generate dollar-for-dollar discounts without limit above $10,000,000 of investment.

The lease commences 'upon termination or expiration of the Term', although Section 3.6.1 makes the underlying right arise only on expiration and Section 3.6.2 denies it where MTC terminates for cause.
'MTC's policies then applicable to others' and 'then-prevailing prices' leave the Operator's post-term costs to be set unilaterally later.

'half the actual maintenance costs ... during the last two full calendar year prior to the exercise' is ungrammatical and does not say whether the baseline is half of one year or half of the two-year total.

The stated formula divides maintenance costs by total fiber miles and multiplies by a strand ratio and actual mileage, which does not reproduce 'a pro rata share ... based on the percentage of strands' as the same Section describes it.
Section 3.6.1.5(b) prices the exercise 'regardless of disclaimers of use made pursuant to Section 3.6.1.11', which is difficult to reconcile with disclaimed rights being wholly void here.

The trailing condition 'and the Network Operator has invested less than $3,000,000' is placed so that it may qualify only limb (b) or both limbs, and 'In either such event' then refers back to two limbs of uncertain content.

Section 3.6.1.4 assumes an Operator-initiated non-renewal still yields dark fiber rights priced from $3,000,000 upward, which is hard to square with this Section's forfeiture in the same circumstances.

'responsible for all aspects of the management, sales, monitoring, operations, support, and maintenance' followed by responsibilities that 'include, generally' leaves the enumerated list's relationship to the general grant unresolved.

'Attachment Database' and 'Fiber Management Plan' obligations are imposed here from the Effective Date, but Section 4.3.4 makes the Operator responsible for the Attachment Database only from the Commencement Date.
'Initial Plan' is capitalised here but Section 4.9.3.1 refers only to 'an initial plan', and no definition of the term appears in Article 2.
Section 4.5.2 requires the Fiber Management Plan draft within six months 'after execution of this Agreement' while 4.1.10.4 measures the same six months from the Effective Date.
'shall be reasonably adjusted' fixes no mechanism, no adjuster and no measure of the adjustment.

MTC's sole responsibility for design and construction sits against Section 4.9.2.9, in which MTC only agrees to take 'commercially reasonable steps' toward a design facilitating the Operator's performance.
'promptly after the Effective Date' and 'in such detail as MTC may reasonably request' set no measurable standard for the marketing obligation.

Deemed acceptance runs from 'receipt of such results', but MTC is only obliged to give notice of testing 'when doing so will not adversely impact the construction schedule', so the Operator may be deemed to accept tests it never learned of.

The direction that Article 11's time periods 'shall be reduced by eighty percent (80%)' cannot be applied coherently to Article 11's structure, which fixes a fifteen, thirty and forty-five day escalation ladder and arbitrator-selection windows.

The Operator must perform additional services if MTC 'requires' them while the Parties merely 'shall negotiate an amendment ... that affords commercially reasonable terms', an agreement to agree on price after performance.
'all information, material, documentation, and reports that may be reasonably required or requested by MTC' is an open-ended assistance obligation followed by illustrative specifics.
The Ramp-Up Plan requires 'approval by MTC, EOPSS and ITD', two of whom are not parties, and the contents 'need not be limited to' the listed items.

Section 4.1.10.6 requires the Ramp-Up Plan draft 'within 9 months of the Effective Date' while this Section requires submission within nine months of a start date thirty days after the Effective Date.
'The Parties intend that ...' states purpose rather than obligation, and 'reasonable accommodation' is not defined.
The intention that ITD and EOPSS bear activities outside the demarcation point depends on the demarcation definition that Section 4.5.2.4 leaves to be settled later in the Fiber Management Plan.

Responsibility commences on segment acceptance, whereas Section 4.9.1 makes the Operator pay all operating costs from the Effective Date and Section 4.9.6 keys the CAPEX payments to the Commencement Date.
'the Contract Price' is capitalised but nowhere defined, and the sentence ends with a stray double period.
Article 2 states that all capitalised terms take their meaning from that Article, yet 'Contract Price' and the Design-Build Contractor's agreement terms are not defined there.
The 'Attachment Database' is defined only by reference to a separate agreement with a third-party project manager to which the Operator is not a party.
Section 4.1.2 already obliges the Operator to maintain records in the Attachment Database as a general Article 4 responsibility, while this Section starts that duty only at the Commencement Date.
'the then-current version of Exhibit G' contemplates that the exhibit may change, without saying who may change it or how.
Section 12.1 permits modification of the Agreement only by a signed writing, which is hard to square with an exhibit having a shifting 'then-current version'.
'mutually and regularly consult' imposes no measurable frequency or consequence.

The six-month clock here runs from 'execution of this Agreement' while Section 4.1.10.4 runs the same deadline from the Effective Date, and Section 2.15 defines the Effective Date by a blank in the preamble.
The Section states only when MTC 'will not approve' the plan and never says MTC must approve one that satisfies the listed criteria, and 'excessive stranded segments' has no measure.
Section 12.13.1 requires consents not to be unreasonably withheld, which pulls against a provision framed entirely as grounds for refusal.
'Except as otherwise expressly provided in this Section' is ambiguous as to whether 'this Section' means 4.5.4 alone or the whole of Section 4.5, which determines whether 4.5.5 is carved out.
Section 4.5.5 makes Network Operator Network Extensions 'the sole property of the Network Operator', which the narrower reading of this exception would contradict.
'to expand beyond the MTC Network' does not say how an extension that is physically attached to and served by the MTC Network is distinguished from part of it.

Section 2.39 makes any fiber extension part of the MTC Network unless the Operator proves otherwise, which cannot be squared with an extension being 'the sole property of the Network Operator' by default here.
'qualified contractors' sets no standard and the Section does not say who pays for the Interconnection work.
Customer-funded extensions are the customer's sole property, yet Section 2.39 provides that a fiber extension becomes part of the MTC Network unless the Network Operator establishes otherwise.
'the same role and rights relative to the MBI Network Extensions as are set forth in section 4.2' imports an advisory role written for the initial construction into a different context.

MTC owns any MBI Network Extension 'regardless of the source of its funding', which cannot be squared with Section 2.36's definition requiring MTC funding in whole or in part, nor with Section 4.5.6.3's customer ownership.
'carrier-grade quality and reliability' fixes no measurable upgrade obligation, and the Section both requires periodic upgrades and caps them at available fund balances.

The upgrade duty is funded only from the CAPEX Fund under Section 4.9.6, but Section 4.9.1 makes the Operator pay 'all ongoing costs of operating the MTC Network', leaving the boundary between the two contested.
Tasks 'whether or not specifically described in this Agreement' are deemed included if 'required for the proper performance and provision of the Services', an open-ended sweep-in with no boundary.
This implied-scope rule pulls against Section 12.1, which makes the written Agreement the entire agreement and permits change only by signed writing.
The Section caps rates by reference both to 'Price Caps in Exhibit F' and, for state agencies, to '85% of the applicable rates in the then-current Price Schedule', two different benchmarks.
The Agreement's exhibit list places the Price Caps in Exhibit D and assigns Exhibit F to the Master Services Agreement with EOPSS and ITD, so the cross-reference here points to the wrong exhibit.

The present assignment of all Third Party Service Provider contracts to MTC on termination sits against Section 12.10, which bars assignment of the Agreement without consent and requires assignees expressly to assume obligations.

The Operator acts as MTC's agent for dark fiber leases, yet Section 4.7.4.5 gives it 50% of the payments and Section 2.45 treats that share as its own Network Revenue, which is difficult to square with a pure agency.

'at a the price of $60/mile/strand/month' is ungrammatical, and 'as the same may be adjusted from time to time in accordance with this Agreement' leaves it unclear whether the fixed figure or the Price Schedule governs.
The reference to 'the Pricing Schedule' does not match the defined term 'Price Schedule' in Section 2.53, and a fixed $60 rate sits against the Price Caps regime in Sections 2.52 and 4.7.5.
A compliant lease still requires MTC approval here, which sits against Section 4.7.4.1's premise that standard terms have already been 'approved in advance by MTC'.
'with the expectation that' federal national-security leases 'will be accommodated' and that 'favorable consideration will be given' creates obligations of uncertain force.

The Operator leases extension fiber 'in its own name' and keeps the revenue, while Section 2.45 excludes such revenue and Section 4.7.4.5 splits only MTC Network dark fiber payments, so contiguous circuits may fall on either side.

The 50/50 split of IRU payments must be read together with Section 2.45, which both includes the Operator's share in Network Revenue and excludes MTC's share, so lump-sum IRU payments are shared but then re-shared under Section 4.9.5.

The Price Caps are said to be 'set forth in Exhibit F' although the Agreement's exhibit list assigns Price Caps to Exhibit D, and the amendment route 'pursuant to ARTICLE 6' conflicts with Section 6.2's requirement of written approval of both Parties.
Publication of the Price Schedule sits against Section 2.9(b), which treats fee structures as Confidential Information.
'To the extent requested by the Network Operator' makes the annual update optional, while the following sentence assumes increases will occur and conditions only above-CPI increases on approval.

Allowing Price Caps to be updated annually on the Operator's request conflicts with Section 4.7.5, which makes Exhibit F amendable only pursuant to Article 6, and with Section 6.2's requirement of written approval of both Parties.

The prohibition 'Network Operator shall not provide Retail Services' is self-defeating because Section 2.57 defines Retail Service as services provided by a Third Party Service Provider, which Section 2.64 defines to exclude the Network Operator.

MTC's audit right over an Affiliate's 'Retail Service activities' reaches a non-party, which sits against Section 12.11's bar on conferring rights on non-parties and against Section 12.10's assignment limits.

'all other operating and monitoring expenses contemplated by this Agreement' is a general catch-all closing a long enumerated list, and its reach against the enumerated exclusions that follow is contestable.

The Operator pays 'all ongoing costs of operating the MTC Network' while Section 4.6.1 funds updates and upgrades from the CAPEX Fund held by MTC, leaving the boundary between operating cost and capital upgrade unresolved.
Agreements are provided 'for informational purposes only', yet Section 4.9.2.4 makes previously disclosed terms the benchmark for identifying materially different terms.
'the responsibilities described in this Agreement' with respect to unidentified draft agreements does not specify what those responsibilities are.

'other purposes aimed at maintaining or enhancing the extent, structure, functioning and viability of the MTC Network, including but not limited to' is an open-ended catch-all that expands the Operator's future obligations without limit.
The estimate must compare the proposed term 'with the most expensive alternative contractual term recommended by Network Operator', a comparator that perversely minimises the measured increment.
The Section makes the estimate 'a precondition to exercising the right to object set forth in Section 4.9.2.5', but Section 4.9.2.5 confers a credit and creates no right to object.

The credit is for costs incurred 'as a result of MTC's agreeing to the contractual term objected to', although the Section itself provides no objection procedure and 'shall be entitled take a credit' omits a word.
Section 4.9.2.4 conditions a 'right to object' on the cost estimate, but no such right is created here or anywhere else in the Agreement.

The Operator is MTC's agent but has no authority to modify third-party agreements, which sits against Sections 4.1.8 and 4.1.9 making it 'administratively responsible for ensuring compliance' with those agreements.

Reduction 'in proportion to the average shortfall (from 90%) in the percentage of CAIs that have been connected as of the end of each week' is a formula whose application to a payment amount is not stated.
The reduction applies to payments under Section 4.9.6, but those CAPEX payments begin only after the Commencement Date, so there are no such payments in the window this Section addresses.
'MTC represents and agrees that it will seek advice ... and take commercially reasonable steps' blends a representation with a future covenant of uncertain content.
Section 4.2.1 makes MTC 'solely responsible' for design decisions, which sits against this promise that the network will be designed to facilitate the Operator's achievement of its parameters.

Section 4.1.10.1 calls the same document the 'Initial Plan' as a capitalised term, while this Section refers only to 'an initial plan' and Section 2.4 defines the separate 'Annual Plan' by reference to Section 4.9.2.
'Beginning with the first business day of the fourth quarter ... and by the beginning of each fourth calendar quarter thereafter' is an awkward formulation of an annual deadline.
Section 2.4 defines the Annual Plan as the plan submitted 'pursuant to Section 4.9.2', not this Section, so the defined term points elsewhere.
'paid annually in four (4) equal parts at the beginning of each calendar quarter, commencing with the Effective Date' does not say whether 'Year 1' runs from the Effective Date or by calendar year.
The footnote escalates by 'the CPI' for years beyond Year 10, while Section 4.9.4.2 supplies a different multiplier expressed as 100 plus the CPI increase.

'100 plus the increase in CPI ... stated as a percentage' is ambiguous between the index-point rise and the percentage rise, and the worked example (150 to 165 giving 110%) shows the text does not say what it means.
The same methodology is imported by Sections 3.6.1.5(a), 3.6.1.10 and 4.7.5.2, so the ambiguity propagates into dark-fibre pricing and price-schedule increases.
'CPI Escalation' is capitalised and used as though defined, but no such term appears in Article 2 or elsewhere.

The three tiers are joined by 'plus', which supports a marginal-rate reading, but each is phrased as a percentage 'on annual Network Revenue greater than' a threshold, which supports a whole-amount reading.
Payment is due within 45 days after the Operator's fiscal year, while Section 4.9.8 states that any payment to MTC 'shall be paid quarterly unless another payment schedule is specified herein'.
'the amounts reasonably required for the purposes of the Fund' governs when MTC may divert excess money, without any mechanism for determining that amount.
Section 4.6.1 makes the Fund the source of the Operator's mandatory upgrade obligations, yet this Section allows MTC to spend excess Fund money on other network purposes.

The decommissioning contribution is payable 'within thirty (30) days after the end of each calendar year' but is described as funding decommissioning 'at such other time as MTC determines', with MTC free in its 'sole discretion' to spend the money on anything within MBI's mission.

Payments start 'on the Effective Date' whereas Section 4.9.8 provides that payments to MTC are quarterly unless otherwise specified, and Section 4.9.6 keys the parallel CAPEX contribution to the Commencement Date.
The quarterly default is displaced by annual payment dates in Sections 4.9.5 and 4.9.7, so the provision only operates residually and its field of application is unclear.
'assets, liabilities, income expenses' omits a conjunction, and 'sufficient information and analysis' to MTC's 'reasonable satisfaction' sets no defined deliverable.
'no fraud or intentional or willful misconduct by any Person' certifies as to persons outside the Operator's knowledge, and 'Person' is capitalised but undefined.

The restriction combines a duration test ('more than two (2) years') with an IFRS revenue-recognition test in a single sentence, so it is unclear whether both conditions must be met or either suffices.

The maintenance standard is set by specifications 'contained or incorporated, or to be contained or incorporated, in MTC's agreement with its Design-Build Contractor' and by 'the standards for carrier class networks', neither of which is fixed in this instrument.
The Operator is bound to specifications in a contract to which it is not a party, while Section 12.1 makes this Agreement the entire agreement on the Services.

'appropriate Scheduled Maintenance' measured by the Operator's own 'then current preventative maintenance procedures, which shall meet or exceed standard industry practice' allows the obligor to set its own standard.
'MTC may not prevent Network Operator from performing maintenance that Network Operator deems necessary' is absolute, and the following sentence calls MTC's right to be present 'this requirement'.

The unqualified statement that MTC may not prevent maintenance sits against Section 4.1's reservation of 'reasonable oversight by MTC' and Section 4.11.7's requirement of an MTC-approved procedures manual.
'any potential service-affecting situation' and 'any event imminently likely to cause' failure set no ascertainable trigger for the emergency and non-emergency categories.
'credible notification by any third party' is an undefined standard for triggering dispatch.
'workmanlike care' and 'reasonably cooperate ... in analyzing the disturbances' are open-textured standards with no benchmark.
Section 5.1.8 promises performance 'in accordance with or exceeding generally accepted industry standards', a different and higher standard than 'workmanlike care' here.
The manual must 'ensure that SLAs are met' although Section 4.13.1 records that the SLA was still being completed when the Agreement was signed.
'such information and documentation ... that may be required' identifies the obligation only by reference to unspecified future insurance and recovery needs.
'a claim or series of claims arising out of a single event totaling more than $500,000' does not say whether the threshold is measured by claimed amount, settled amount or proceeds.
Proceeds must be applied to repair or replacement here, while Section 4.11.8.2 and Section 2.45 divert rental-loss proceeds into Network Revenue subject to revenue sharing.
'net of legal fees or other extraordinary costs of recovery outside of normal claim adjustment costs' draws a line between normal and extraordinary costs that is nowhere defined.
Section 2.45 states that Network Revenue 'shall include the proceeds of any rental loss insurance coverage', without the net-of-costs qualification this Section adds.
'as quickly as possible (allowing for delays caused by circumstances beyond the reasonable control of Network Operator)' sets a response standard with no measurable content.
This open-ended standard sits against the specific service levels the SLA is to contain under Section 4.13.1 and the KPI regime of Section 4.13.3.
Free subcontracting of maintenance sits against Section 12.10's prohibition on assigning the Agreement in whole or in part without consent.
'Segments of the MTC Network' is capitalised as if referring to the defined 'Network Segment', and the Section does not say who bears the cost of the testing MTC directs.
'full compliance with all Network Policies' is absolute, but Section 2.44 lets MTC add policies unilaterally and Section 4.7.4.1 lets MTC exempt dark fiber leases from them.
The performance standard is fixed by 'the SLA the Parties are in the process of completing', a document that did not exist at signing, so the operative standard was left to future agreement.
The cross-reference to Sections 4.9.2.4 and 4.9.2.5 is astray: those provisions govern MTC's agreements with third parties and an incremental-cost credit, not the completion of the SLA.
'will review and agree to commercially reasonable changes' is an agreement to agree, resolved only by a further duty to 'deal with each other in good faith'.
The Section gives no route to resolution if the Parties do not agree, which sits against Section 6.2's requirement of express written approval of both Parties for any change.
Performance is measured against KPIs 'as the same may evolve and be supplemented and enhanced during the Term', without saying who may change them.
Section 6.1.1(ii) gives the IPT only a recommending role over KPIs, and Section 6.2 requires both Parties' written approval, so unilateral evolution of KPIs is not supported.

Records must be kept 'at least seven (7) years after the end of the Term' here, while Section 4.1.3 requires seven years 'beyond the Term' and Section 3.6.1.2 requires seven years for discount documentation, creating overlapping regimes.
'Network Operator shall promptly make all remunerative payments to MTC' uses 'remunerative' in an unnatural sense and provides no reciprocal adjustment where the error favours MTC.
A twenty-four hour notice requirement here sits against Section 4.14.1's grant of access 'at all reasonable times' without notice.
'any changes and take other actions which are necessary in order to maintain compliance' is unbounded and does not address who bears the cost.
'unless expressly constructed otherwise' is a mechanical error for 'construed', and the sentence turns on which reading is taken.
The denial of any leasehold or similar interest sits against Section 3.6.1, which grants the Operator a right to lease dark fiber through an IRU on the same network.
'necessary or appropriate' resources 'however described' is an open-ended cost allocation with no boundary.
The general duty to pay for all resources sits against Section 4.6.1's CAPEX Fund mechanism and Section 4.9.1's carve-outs for construction and MBI Extension costs.
'an adequate number of trained and qualified personnel as necessary or appropriate' fixes no measurable staffing obligation.
'reasonable access' 'as necessary or appropriate' does not say whether MTC may condition or refuse access the Operator considers essential.
'an office ... which shall be the headquarters for the Network Operator' does not say whether the corporate headquarters must relocate to Massachusetts or only a project office be maintained.
Section 12.12.2 gives the Operator's notice address in Calgary, Alberta, which sits awkwardly with a covenant that its headquarters be in Massachusetts.
'in line with industry best practices' and 'no less stringent than the then-current requirements of MassDOT, ITD and EOPSS' import moving external standards with no fixed content.
The duty to 'deny such access to all other persons' sits against Section 4.14.1, which requires access for MTC's auditors, inspectors, regulators and other designated representatives.
'a legal, valid and binding obligation of such Party' uses 'such Party' with no antecedent in a representation made only by the Network Operator.
Section 12.14 makes the Agreement binding 'only upon condition that' the parent delivers a guaranty, which sits against an unqualified representation that the Agreement is already binding.

The representation covers the parent company and 'any of their respective officers, directors or Affiliates', a class the Operator cannot fully know, and 'threatened' criminal investigations have no defined test.
The representation is stated to continue 'throughout the Term', which cannot literally be true of a warranty as to conduct 'at all times since January 1, 2005'.
'services that are substantially equivalent to the Services in other settings and circumstances' is a warranty of past experience with no measurable content.
'in accordance with or exceeding generally accepted industry standards' is an undefined benchmark.
This general industry standard sits against Section 4.13.1's promise to meet the (then unwritten) SLA standards and Section 4.11.6's lower 'workmanlike care'.
The representation is stated to continue throughout the Term although it is framed as to matters 'not disclosed to MTC or its designee prior to the Effective Date'.
'timely and diligently cooperate to effect the goals, objectives and purposes of this Agreement' is an open-ended covenant with no measurable content.
'self-dealing' is undefined and the covenant to protect 'the interests of MTC as owner' in all third-party transactions has no stated boundary.

Section 4.8 expressly permits an Affiliate of the Operator to contract with it as a Third Party Service Provider, and Sections 2.43 and 4.5.5 contemplate the Operator trading with itself on its own Extensions.
The Operator covenants to comply with Article 5 of a Master Services Agreement that was 'currently being negotiated' and therefore had unknown content at signing.

The cross-reference to 'Sections 4.9.2.4 and 4.9.2.5' is astray, as those provisions deal with MTC's negotiation of third-party agreements and an incremental-cost credit, not the finalisation of this covenant.

The representation that all required insurance 'has been taken out' as of the Effective Date sits against Section 10.3.3, which allows thirty days after the Effective Date for certificates and later procurement of some coverages.

'ensure that the MTC Network is and remains, in compliance with all Network Policies, laws, regulations, and orders' is an absolute guarantee of a state of affairs partly outside the Operator's control.
'immediately in writing' sets no ascertainable deadline.
'such Party' has no antecedent within this MTC representation.
Section 12.14 conditions the Agreement's becoming binding on delivery of a parent guaranty, which sits against an unqualified representation that it is already binding.
'timely and diligently cooperate to effect the goals, objectives and purposes of this Agreement' has no measurable content.

Purpose (iv) gives the IPT power 'to resolve disputes submitted by the Parties pursuant to ARTICLE 11', while Section 11.1.1.3 gives it only a duty to discuss and negotiate before escalation and arbitration.

The IPT includes a representative of EOPSS and ITD who are not Parties, yet Section 11.1.3 allows the IPT to stay arbitration time periods 'upon unanimous vote of its members', giving a non-party a veto over the Parties' dispute process.
An IPT that need meet only once a year sits against Section 11.1.1.2, which requires it to 'meet as often as necessary' in a dispute, and against the fifteen-day resolution window in Section 11.1.2.
Limb (ii) says the Parties 'may either negotiate to amend the Agreement ... or consider the change during any subsequent renewal', so no change is ever compelled.
Section 4.7.5 makes the Price Caps amendable 'pursuant to ARTICLE 6', but this Section supplies no mechanism that can produce an amendment without both Parties' agreement.
'promptly deliver to the requesting party any and all Confidential Information' on request 'at any time' is unqualified and would require return of information needed for continued performance.

Each Party being 'the exclusive owner' of its own Confidential Information cannot be squared with Section 7.3.4, which declares all written and electronic materials containing Confidential Information 'the sole and exclusive property of MTC'.

MTC's public-records disclosure obligations sit against Section 2.9's inclusion of 'the existence, terms and conditions of this Agreement' in Confidential Information and against Section 7.3.1's absolute non-disclosure duty.
The Operator must comply with confidentiality policies 'as communicated by MTC's Executive Director or General Counsel ... from time to time', which allows unilateral variation of its obligations.
Unilateral communication of new policy obligations conflicts with Section 12.1, which permits amendment only by written document signed by both Parties.
The exceptions are limited to fulfilment of obligations and General Counsel direction, while Section 7.5 supplies a wider set of exceptions to the same Section 7.3 duties.
'any Person related to or that is an Affiliate of with Network Operator' is ungrammatical, and 'any Applicable Third Party' is capitalised but never defined.
Article 2 provides that all capitalised terms take their meanings from that Article, yet 'Applicable Third Party' appears nowhere in it.
'To the maximum extent required by law, Network Operator shall indemnify' is an odd formulation ('required' rather than 'permitted'), and 'MTC's Written Materials' is capitalised but undefined.
Making all such materials 'the sole and exclusive property of MTC' cannot be squared with Section 7.1, under which each Party exclusively owns the Confidential Information it furnishes.
The exceptions are conditioned on proof 'through written records' and use the undefined capitalised terms 'Governmental Authority' and 'Applicable Third Party'.
The carve-outs are expressed to apply only to 'obligations under Section 7.3', leaving the parallel obligations in Sections 7.1 and 7.2 unqualified.

'a series of non-material or persistent breaches ... that, in the aggregate, have a material and significant adverse impact' has no measurable threshold, and the change-of-control test — control 'through the ownership of at least fifty percent (50%) of the voting securities' — is ambiguous as to whether ownership is required at all.

Termination for cause here drives Section 3.6.1 and 3.6.2, which strip the Operator's dark fiber rights, and Section 8.4.1, which says the Term is not deemed terminated until transfer assistance is complete.

The charge 'increas[es] the percentage of Network Revenue owed ... under Section 4.9.5' by half a point, but Section 4.9.5 contains three different percentages (0%, 4% and 20%), so which percentage is increased is not stated.
The charge is available for any Section 8.1 ground except 8.1.4, yet Sections 8.1.2 and 8.1.3 provide no notice-and-cure period from which the 'initial thirty (30) days' can be measured.
'a disruption to the basic functioning of more than fifty percent (50%) of the MTC Network' gives no measure — by mileage, strands, customers or revenue — for the fifty percent threshold.
'as soon as is reasonably practicable by one acting with urgency' compounds two open standards to fix the extension of time.

This excuse for Force Majeure failures sits against Section 12.2, which excuses nonperformance only where caused by the other Party's default, and against Section 11.2's duty of continued performance.

'Neither the Term ... nor Network Operator's obligations ... shall be deemed to have expired or terminated until the services transfer assistance ... is completed' has no outer limit and no definition of completion.

This open-ended extension cannot be squared with Section 3.1, under which the Term terminates on the tenth anniversary of the Commencement Date, nor with the termination rights in Sections 8.1 and 8.6.
'services transfer assistance, as described herein' is never actually described beyond a duty to 'cooperate', so the content of the obligation is unstated.
Assistance may be required 'upon any notice of termination or of non-renewal of the Agreement pursuant to ARTICLE 3', but Article 3 contains no notice of termination mechanism.

'the effective date of such expiration or termination shall be extended for up to one year' at MTC's request gives one Party a unilateral power to prolong the contract without stating the terms of payment.
A unilateral one-year extension cannot be squared with Section 3.1's fixed Term or with Section 3.2's requirement that renewal be by mutual agreement.
'on mutually acceptable terms and conditions' makes the transfer obligation an agreement to agree, and 'other necessary third party services' is an undefined catch-all after the enumerated examples.

The Operator's right to terminate for MTC's material breach sits against Section 8.4.1, under which its obligations are not deemed terminated until transfer assistance is complete, and Section 11.2's duty of continued performance.

Limb (d) covers any act or omission that causes 'in whole or in part' MTC to breach an agreement with 'any other person relating to the MTC Network', a general catch-all following specific categories of counterparty.
The indemnity runs to 'Affiliates, officers, directors ... successors and assigns' as Indemnified Parties, which sits against Section 12.11's provision that no rights are conferred on non-parties.
MTC's indemnity is markedly narrower than the Operator's under Section 9.1, omitting bodily injury and infringement, so the asymmetry may be argued as deliberate expressio unius.

'So long as the Indemnifying Party is not in default in the performance of its obligations under the Agreement' conditions control of the defence on a default test that is nowhere confined to material default.
Apportionment on 'final adjudication' assumes a court judgment, while Section 11.1.3 makes arbitration a condition precedent to any suit and the arbitrator's award final.
Requiring 'the written approval of both the Parties' for any settlement gives the indemnified Party a veto without any reasonableness qualification.
Section 9.3 gives the Indemnifying Party 'primary responsibility for the conduct of an Indemnified Claim Proceeding', which is hard to square with a mutual settlement veto here.

'and such other coverages as the Parties may determine are commercially reasonable' is an open-ended addition to a carefully enumerated schedule, and 'As and when required' in 10.1.2 leaves the automobile trigger unstated.
Section 10.1.3 requires contractual liability cover only for indemnity obligations under Sections 9.1(a), 9.1(d) and 9.1(e), leaving 9.1(b) and 9.1(c) uninsured though still owed.
'The Parties will confer ... to determine commercially reasonable levels and types of coverage' leaves the property insurance obligation to future agreement with no fallback.
Section 5.1.16 warrants that the Operator 'has taken out all insurance required under this Agreement' as of the Effective Date, which cannot be true of coverage still to be agreed under this Section.
'insuring against all standard perils ... (subject to normal and customary terms, exclusions, sublimits and conditions)' both grants and takes away by reference to undefined market practice.
'in any other sequence of Losses' uses the capitalised term 'Losses', which is not defined in Article 2 or anywhere in the Agreement.
'Where possible' and 'an annual aggregate limit commensurate with the value of the assets in service' leave the required limit unascertainable.
'commercially reasonable deductibles reasonably satisfactory to MTC' combines an objective and a subjective standard without saying which governs.
'so-called "all risk" and "law and ordinance" coverage' incorporates market terms of art whose content is not fixed by the Agreement.
Section 10.2.2 already requires All Risk coverage 'subject to normal and customary ... exclusions', while this Section requires cover 'without limitation' of the listed perils.
'Subject to such further determination as to commercially reasonable amounts, timing, deductibles, and terms' makes the rental loss cover contingent on later agreement.

Section 2.45 treats rental loss proceeds as Network Revenue and Section 4.11.8.2 nets recovery costs from them, so the cover this Section leaves to future agreement drives fixed revenue-share obligations.
'other statutory insurances where it would be inappropriate' is an undefined exception to the additional insured requirement.

The additional-insured requirement is limited to 'the policies listed in Section 10.1', although Section 10.3.4 assumes property policies under Section 10.2 are also within the same regime by naming MTC as loss payee.
A blanket waiver of recovery against MTC sits against Section 9.2, under which MTC indemnifies the Operator for losses from MTC's third-party breaches and non-compliance with law.
The certificate deadlines are internally muddled: complete policies are due within thirty days of the Effective Date 'or policy renewal date', while certificates are due thirty days before expiry.
The opening carve-out 'Except as set forth in Section 10.2.1' points to a provision that says nothing about certificates, and Section 8.1.1 makes a breach of this Section a ten-day cure default.
'a reasonable administrative fee as designated by MTC' lets one Party set its own charge, and 'documenting commercially reasonable types and amounts' of subcontractor insurance fixes no level.

MTC is to be 'named as loss payee' on property policies here, while Section 10.3 limits the additional-insured endorsement to the Section 10.1 liability policies and Section 4.11.8.1 directs proceeds to repair.
The declared refusal to limit the Operator's liability sits against Section 12.14, which caps the parent guaranty at $4,000,000.

The cross-reference to 'agreements between MTC and others that are within the scope of Section 4.1' is astray, since agreements between MTC and third parties are the subject of Section 4.9.2, not Section 4.1.

'Any dispute between the Parties either with respect to the interpretation of any provision ... or with respect to the performance' fixes the scope of a mandatory dispute regime, and the closing words 'regardless of whether or not mention of this Article is made in any other Section' extend it to matters not expressly referred.

Because 'Party' is defined in Section 2.50 as only MTC and the Network Operator, this clause does not reach the parent guarantor whose guaranty Section 12.14 requires, leaving the forum for guaranty disputes unresolved.
'appropriate and germane' sets no standard for what information the IPT must gather and furnish.
The duty to meet 'as often as necessary' sits against Section 6.1.3, under which the IPT need meet only once a year.
The IPT is only to 'discuss the problem and negotiate in good faith' here, while Section 6.1.1(iv) states that its purpose includes resolving disputes submitted under Article 11.
'all reasonable requests ... for non-privileged information reasonably related to the Agreement, will be honored' is a disclosure duty with no stated limit or timeframe.
The obligation to honour information requests sits against the confidentiality restrictions of Article 7 and Section 9.4's express subjection of records to those limits.
The escalation runs from 'receipt by the other Party of the Dispute Resolution Notice', so the fifteen-day and thirty-day periods overlap and the officers' window shrinks to fifteen days.
Section 11.1.3 then measures the arbitration trigger from forty-five days after the same notice, so the three deadlines in Article 11 all run from one date and must be harmonised.

'Except in the case of an emergency, exhaustion of the foregoing procedures shall be a condition precedent' leaves 'emergency' undefined, and the clause both makes arbitration a condition precedent to any suit and carves out 'applications to courts of competent jurisdiction for injunctive relief'.

The clause binds only 'the Parties' as defined in Section 2.50, so its application to the parent guaranty required by Section 12.14 — and its interaction with Section 11.1.4's court route and Section 11.2's continued performance duty — is left open.
'would permit or cause irreparable injury ... due to delay arising out of the dispute resolution process' is a self-judging condition on immediate resort to court.

This open court route cannot easily be squared with Section 11.1.3, which makes arbitration a condition precedent to 'any suit, action or proceeding instituted in any court', subject only to a narrower injunctive-relief carve-out.
'unless otherwise directed by MTC' allows one Party unilaterally to suspend the other's performance obligations while a dispute is pending, without limit or standard.
A duty to keep performing 'while the dispute is being resolved' cannot easily be squared with the termination rights in Sections 8.1 and 8.6 or with Section 8.4.1's transfer-assistance regime.
The merger clause is limited to 'the Services and matters addressed therein', leaving open what other agreements between these Parties survive.

The clause sits against Section 12.14's parent guaranty, Section 4.13.1's yet-to-be-completed SLA and Section 4.7.4.1's incorporation of Network Policies, all of which are documents outside the signed text.
'Time is of the essence' is stated without qualification alongside an excuse for nonperformance caused by the other Party, leaving the two rules to be reconciled.
The excuse is limited to 'nonmonetary obligations', which sits against Section 4.9.2.8's monetary reduction for MTC-caused delay and Section 4.1.11's adjustment of deliverable dates.

'any other provisions that by their terms cannot be performed prior to the expiration or earlier termination' is a general catch-all following two named Articles, so which other provisions survive is contestable.
Article 3.6's post-term dark fiber rights, Article 7's post-termination confidentiality duties and Section 8.4's transfer assistance are all intended to survive but are not among the named survivors.
'such provision shall be deemed to be restated to reflect the Parties' original intentions as nearly as possible' invites a court to rewrite rather than sever an invalid term.

The choice of Massachusetts law for 'any and all claims and disputes arising out of ... the relationships and arrangements between MTC and Network Operator' overlaps with Section 11.1.3's own choice-of-law direction to the arbitrator, and neither addresses the parent guaranty required by Section 12.14.

The permitted assignees are 'another entity of the Commonwealth, a subsidiary of MTC or a special purpose entity', but the notice sentence then speaks of assignment 'to an Affiliate', a different and undefined class here.

The bar on assignment without consent sits against Section 4.7.3, which effects a present assignment of Third Party Service Provider contracts to MTC on termination, and against Section 8.5.1's transfer obligations.

The bar on third-party rights cannot easily be squared with Section 2.24 and Article 9, which confer indemnity rights on Affiliates, officers and directors, or with Section 10.3's naming of MassDOT and its bond trustees as additional insureds.
Limb (e) — 'when received electronically if sent by email and one of the delivery methods in (a) through (d) above' — is garbled and does not say whether email alone is ever effective.
Section 4.2.4 permits acceptance-test challenges to be 'transmitted electronically', which sits against a notice clause that appears to require email to be paired with another method.

A general duty not to withhold consent unreasonably sits against provisions giving MTC 'sole discretion' (Sections 2.7 and 4.9.7) and against Section 4.5.3's grounds for refusing approval of the Fiber Management Plan.

The proviso 'that Network Operator shall be subject to any application or access fees and that such policies and procedures MassDOT has agreed with MTC to apply in a non-discriminatory manner' is ungrammatical and appears to have dropped a negative, so it reads against the interest the proviso was meant to protect.

The final sentence makes it 'the sole responsibility of Network Operator to obtain all governmental approvals for any Alterations to be done by or on behalf of MTC', which cannot be squared with Section 4.2.1's allocation of permitting responsibility to MTC and its vendors.

'use all reasonable efforts to limit the rights and obligations of Network Operator so that it does not become a subrecipient of the Grant' sets an aim that could require cutting back rights and duties conferred elsewhere, without saying which.

The direction to limit the Operator's rights and obligations sits against the extensive fixed obligations of Article 4 and the dark fiber rights of Section 3.6, and against Section 12.1's rule that changes require a signed writing.

'This Agreement shall become binding only upon condition that' the parent delivers a guaranty 'in a form acceptable to MTC' leaves both the condition's satisfaction and the guaranty's terms to MTC's later judgment.

The guaranty is a separate instrument whose disputes are not obviously caught by Article 11, which covers only disputes 'between the Parties' as defined in Section 2.50, and Section 12.11 denies rights to non-parties.
